issues.legal_issue: A tenant who entered premises before they became public premises may become an unauthorised occupant when the tenancy is validly determined and the tenant continues to occupy them.
material_facts: The occupant had been inducted as a tenant by the prior private owner before the premises were acquired by a public corporation.
After acquiring the premises, the corporation gave a notice determining the tenancy; the validity of that notice was not challenged for deciding this issue.
The occupant continued to occupy the premises after the tenancy was determined and after the public-premises eviction law came into force.
issues.conclusion: The occupant was in unauthorised occupation, and the Estate Officer could proceed under the public-premises eviction law.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(2)(g) of the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971 concerns occupation, a continuing state, and expressly includes continued occupation after the authority to occupy has expired or been determined. A tenant's original lawful entry does not prevent later occupation from being unauthorised once the tenancy is determined. Raj Kumar Devendra Singh v. State of Punjab was distinguished because the Punjab statute focused on entry into possession, unlike section 2(2)(g); the court also relied on the notice determining the tenancy under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act.

rule.if: public_premises_eviction_proceeding and occupant_entered_under_tenancy_before_public_ownership and tenancy_validly_determined and occupant_continued_occupying

predicates.public_premises_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction through a special process for premises belonging to a public body.
predicates.occupant_entered_under_tenancy_before_pu: The occupant first took possession lawfully as a tenant before the premises became publicly owned.
predicates.tenancy_validly_determined: The landlord validly ended the occupant's authority to remain under the tenancy.
predicates.occupant_continued_occupying: The occupant remained in the premises after that authority ended.

issues.definition: When a public-premises eviction proceeding concerns a former tenant who remains after a valid termination of the tenancy, the occupant is unauthorised.

issues.legal_issue: The special eviction regime for public premises prevails over the general tenant-protection regime where their application overlaps.
material_facts: The premises were owned by a public corporation and fell within the public-premises eviction regime.
The occupant argued that the tenant-protection law barred recovery of possession except through its own procedure.
The public-premises law was enacted after the tenant-protection law, although it was given retrospective effect from an earlier date.
The public-premises law applied to a limited class of publicly owned premises and provided a summary eviction procedure; the tenant-protection law had broader application.
issues.conclusion: The public-premises eviction law overrides the tenant-protection law, and the latter does not bar proceedings under the former for premises within its scope.
issues.legal_principle: The court considered sections 14, 3(a), and 25B of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, and the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. It held that retrospective operation does not change the actual date of enactment; the later, limited and special public-premises regime prevails over the broader tenant-protection regime. Conflicts between laws containing overriding clauses are resolved by their objects, purposes, and policies. The court relied on Sarwan Singh v. Kasturi Lal and Shri Ram Narain v. The Simla Banking & Industrial Co. Ltd.; it also referred to Northern India Caterers Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Punjab and Maganlal Chhagganlal (P) Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay regarding the distinct class covered and the summary procedure.

predicates.public_premises_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction under a special regime for publicly owned premises.
predicates.premises_belong_to_covered_public_body: The premises belong to a public body covered by the special eviction regime.
predicates.limited_public_property_eviction_regime_: A later-enacted regime provides a distinct eviction process for a limited class of publicly owned premises.
predicates.overlapping_tenant_protection_regime_is_: A separate tenant-protection regime covers a wider range of premises and its procedure overlaps with the public-premises process.

issues.definition: Where a proceeding concerns premises covered by a limited, special public-property eviction regime and that regime overlaps with a broader tenant-protection regime, the special regime prevails.

issues.legal_issue: The special eviction regime for public premises prevails over a conflicting statutory restriction on eviction proceedings in slum areas.
material_facts: The premises were within the scope of the public-premises eviction regime.
The occupant argued that the slum-area law required prior written permission before instituting eviction proceedings.
The public-premises eviction law was enacted after the slum-area law as amended and prescribed a forum for eviction of unauthorised occupants of covered premises.
The court found the two regimes directly in conflict and treated the public-premises law as a later law with a limited, special scope.
issues.conclusion: The public-premises eviction law overrides the conflicting slum-area restriction for premises within its scope.
issues.legal_principle: Section 19 of the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956, as amended, required prior written permission to institute certain eviction proceedings concerning buildings or land in slum areas. The court held that this requirement directly conflicted with the forum and eviction process provided for covered premises by the later Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. Applying the same reasoning used to resolve the conflict with the tenant-protection law, the later and specially limited public-premises regime prevailed.

rule.if: public_premises_eviction_proceeding and premises_within_special_public_eviction_regime and slum_area_eviction_restriction_applies and eviction_regimes_directly_conflict and public_eviction_regime_is_later_and_limited

predicates.public_premises_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction under a special regime for publicly owned premises.
predicates.premises_within_special_public_eviction_: The premises are covered by the special public-premises eviction regime.
predicates.slum_area_eviction_restriction_applies: A separate rule requires prior permission before instituting eviction proceedings concerning the premises.
predicates.eviction_regimes_directly_conflict: The permission requirement conflicts with the forum or process prescribed by the public-premises regime.

issues.definition: When a later, limited public-premises eviction regime directly conflicts with a permission requirement for eviction proceedings, the public-premises regime prevails.
